blocks.x: Unity has released its official plugin for Grok Build, bringing its engineering guidance directly to the terminal. One command installs it, with no manual setup, and it works out of the box with Unity 6 and above.

The plugin carries 30+ Unity skills written by Unity feature teams, covering areas such as UI Toolkit, URP, Shader Graph, physics, LevelPlay and localization, plus Unity CLI workflows that let the agent drive a running Unity Editor and build and test projects.

According to Unity's blog, Grok Build is the third coding agent to get the plugin after Claude Code and Codex. The skills are identical across all three and maintained from a single repository, so every agent gives the same Unity guidance for the same question. Unity says it will publish data on how developers use the CLI and plugin with these agents in October.

A community creator has released v1.84 of the UEFN Claude Team Starter Kit, which turns a Claude Code + Unreal MCP setup for UEFN into a working AI dev team with a live dashboard. It is free and open source.

The Agent Console shows 12 specialist agents (coder, reviewers, QA, release gate, planner and more) with every handoff visible in real time, alongside island stats such as plays, D1/D7 retention and genre rank. The team also writes and updates the spec, roadmap and bug backlog as it works.

Every lesson is proposed, never applied silently, and a pattern becomes "proven" only when it holds across several maps. Projects also update themselves from a template at the start of each session.

On the Snarketing Podcast, Twitch CEO Dan Clancy said that because the site already transcribes streams, it has "lately been using AI to also identify streamers that may not match a brand" so ads can be pulled from broadcasts that don't fit an advertiser's considerations.

Streamers are not enthused. "Ohhh so that's why ad revenue dropped," said JP "itmeJP" McDaniel, while Vtuber LuminusRed worried that being a lesbian could cause the AI to remove ads. Others asked whether creators will ever learn what they were flagged for.

In an update, a Twitch representative told Aftermath that each advertiser sets its own preferences and that better matching should open up more ad opportunities. "Twitch staff reviews flagged content at multiple stages, and as always, any changes to longer term ad eligibility would be a human decision," the rep said, adding that Twitch is building ways to tell creators when advertiser preferences affect their revenue.
Aftermath argues questions remain about what standards the AI follows and where accountability lies.
I've been building a plugin that links any UE5 project to a local AI "brain", so a MetaHuman can talk and act inside the level, with no cloud AI.
In this demo she's a safety trainer: she walks to an electric motor, explains its controls, and presses the buttons herself, so the motor really starts and stops.

Body motion is generated live by NVIDIA's ARDY (text-to-motion) and retargeted onto the MetaHuman, with no animation assets. Walking uses the generated root motion along the NavMesh, so the feet don't slide.

She operates the level by calling its own Blueprint functions (StartMotor, StopMotor…). The plugin discovers them automatically and reads the Blueprint's variables (IsRunning, EmergencyLatched) and its Print String messages, so she knows when a machine refuses (e.g. "press RESET first").

Tap anything on the stream to ask "what is this?" or "go there" (line trace from the view). Phoneme-timed lip sync, facial expressions, a portrait light rig that follows the camera, and a face close-up with depth of field. Pixel Streaming to phones, plus a JavaScript API (e.g. setExpression("uncertain", 0.4)).
The AI side runs on the same machine (one RTX GPU): local speech recognition, a local LLM, neural TTS, and a knowledge graph built from the company's own documents.
Feedback is very welcome, especially on the motion and the lip sync!

AI 3D generation platform Meshy has unveiled the details of 'Mora' (Multimodal Open-world Real-time Architecture). The idea is to generate an entire world that people can walk through, play in, and interact with in real time. The early demo, Mora 1, is open to anyone at mora.fun. It includes spatial puzzles, multiplayer platformers, building, racing, and sports, and the visual style can be changed.

The industry has largely relied on having a single video model simulate the entire world from start to finish. But this approach still struggles to keep space consistent and support complex interactions. Mora's idea is different: a world should be built first, then rendered.

So the work is split into layers. A coding agent writes the logic and mechanics that run the world, while Meshy's 3D generation builds the spatial structure and assets. A real-time video model then applies the final visuals and sound. Game rules stay intact and space stays persistent, and visual quality improves as the video model advances through generations. Because each layer develops separately, any progress in the coding agent, 3D generation, or video model accumulates inside Mora.
Mora 1 is an early research demo meant to validate this architecture. A general-purpose world-building tool remains a more distant goal, and Mora 2 is in development.

blocks.cap: A Meshy 7.1 result made from a single image, comparing the Standard, Ultra 2K, and Ultra 4K outputs side by side.

blocks.x: On September 16, Meshy also released Meshy 7.1, a new version of its flagship image-to-3D model. It is available to all signed-up users and adds new high-detail modes, 'Ultra 2K' and 'Ultra 4K'.

Ultra 4K builds geometry at a 4096³ voxel resolution. The raw mesh before simplification reaches up to 80 million triangles. Meshy said it is the first generative 3D model to reach 4096³ resolution. Details like stitching, fabric weave, and individual scales are built as mesh geometry rather than textures, making it useful for 3D printing or digital sculpting work.

In the company's new internal 'Detail Richness Benchmark' evaluation, Meshy 7.1 ranked first among five image-to-3D models across all three rendering resolutions. A paid subscription is required for Ultra modes and for downloading the 7.1 model. Ultra 2K supports both single- and multi-view generation, while Ultra 4K currently supports single-view only.

Typical AI video generation is a one-shot process. It takes a prompt, produces a clip of fixed length, and stops. To fix anything, you have to start over with a new prompt. Real-time world models are different. Instead of a clip, they generate a world that keeps running for as long as the user stays, and input that arrives during generation changes the next scene.

PixVerse released its first real-time world model, R1, in January 2026. R2 is the upgrade. It maintains consistency over much longer sessions, remembers and carries forward what happened within a session, and accepts text, reference, audio, and action controls into the same world.

The key is that input persists. Previously, input affected only that moment and then vanished. In R2, a prompt, action, or audio signal changes the state of the world itself, shaping how characters behave later and how situations play out.
Players move through the world using WASD keys to control the character and arrow keys to control the camera. They can also add elements or change the environment with prompts while moving.

In 'Zero Mark,' an interactive cinematic game that creator Xiaolongbao made with R2, a monster blocks the path and demands a gift. Giving it a dragon versus a leaf leads to completely different reactions, and the model generates the outcome on the spot.

blocks.cap: The same scene in 'Zero Mark' splits into two branches depending on whether the player gives a dragon or a leaf.

blocks.x: Speed and performance usually trade off against each other. Instead of choosing one, R2 splits the work into two stages. 'Omni Causal AR' scales up performance as a continuously learning backbone, while a real-time acceleration layer compresses the same model to run in real time.

blocks.cap: R2's architecture replaces a training pipeline that lost quality across multiple stages with a single continuously learning model plus real-time compression.

blocks.x: Co-founder and CEO Changhu Wang said, “Large language models showed that scaling is a reliable path to performance,” adding that R2 is evidence real-time world models can follow the same path. The PixVerse Game Engine, first introduced in July, now runs on top of R2, and worlds made by creators can be explored at world.pixverse.video.

Give Everboard's new 21.5-inch tablet just three words, like “sushi-juggling cat,” and it produces a new game you can play right away. The generative AI-based 'EverVibe Game Creator' makes games that sit on the line between board games and mobile games.

Everboard was announced Thursday morning as a $499.99 digital game table, sold exclusively at Best Buy later this year. The device is a 21.5-inch 1080p touchscreen meant to sit in the middle of a table. It supports 10-point touch for up to six people playing from four directions, and has a built-in battery so it can be carried around.

Players can speak or type the game they want, or choose theme, rules, controls, and visual style from a menu. EverVibe asks a few questions about how many people are playing, where they're sitting, whether a computer opponent is needed, and how controls should work. The company says rules, turn structure, scoring, and win conditions can all be changed, along with the board, characters, art, sound, and music.

Games can be refined with plain language like “make it faster” or “add a power-up.” Every edit is saved as a new version, so if the AI goes in the wrong direction, you can revert to an earlier version. Four privacy films are also included to hide a player's hand on the shared screen.

The AI model comes from what Everboard describes only as an “existing commercial provider.” It has not disclosed which company. An adult handles device setup and decides whether EverVibe is turned on and who can use it. The company says it will not train its AI on players' prompts or creations.

The cost doesn't end with the hardware. The device includes one month of the EverPass subscription service, which unlocks the full library and five Game Creator generations per month. EverPass costs $29 for three months or $99 for a year. EverPass Premium, for $50 more per year, increases the 'generation allowance' fivefold, allowing up to 25 quick games or five advanced games per month, or a mix of both. This limit may change.

Even without a subscription, 10 free basic games are available. The library has more than 50 titles at launch, with Hasbro's Monopoly, Connect 4, Chutes and Ladders, and Scrabble confirmed. Still, skepticism about generative AI persists across the creative industries, and a tool that generates rules, art, and music in its place is unlikely to escape that question.

The UK Games Expo (UKGE), Britain's largest tabletop convention, introduced a new policy on AI-made games this week. The organizers, who had previously been criticized for being too close to AI, reversed course and decided to bar AI games from the show, with only a very narrow exception.

The new policy states: “The organizers reserve the right, at their sole discretion, to require exhibitors displaying, showcasing, or selling such items to remove them. Refusal to comply may result in the closure of the booth and a ban on future participation.”

UKGE, which began in 2007 and is held every summer in Birmingham, is one of the most important events in the tabletop industry. According to Kyle Hoon Chan's report at Rascal, UKGE now bans AI-generated work from the show floor, following the lead of major overseas events like Gen Con. The decision came after mounting frustration. On top of complaints about having to share floor space with vendors selling low-quality AI products, UKGE drew backlash in 2025 for promoting the AI-made 'Gates of Crystalia' in a sponsored social media post. Now staff can remove AI exhibits from the show floor, and other vendors face less suspicion over their own work.

There is one exception. Using AI for “light editing, production assistance, and accessibility” is not banned. While the biggest names in gaming and commercial entertainment are pushing AI hard, the same trend hasn't taken hold in tabletop. Some of the industry's largest companies are taking a hard line instead. Games Workshop, maker of Warhammer, bars employees from using AI in their work (though accusations that it has used AI persist). Other gaming executives hope to cut staff and development costs with AI, but tabletop players may simply hold a special attachment to hand-drawn goblin art and figures they can hold in their hands.

blocks.cap: Needle in a Haystack Simulator (Image: Polden Publishing)

blocks.x: The co-op PC simulation game 'Needle in a Haystack Simulator' is exactly what it sounds like. It went viral on social media this summer, and, predictably, a wave of clones followed.

The whole point is to find a single needle in a massive haystack with friends — true to the old saying, except the hay totals roughly 5 million strands. As soon as it went viral, about eight imitators appeared on Steam in just the first part of last week, and there are many more by now.

There were enough that it drew posts on Twitter, and caught the eye of the original creator. Responding to a screenshot showing a dozen or so clones, Studio Bitdot's Nas replied, “As the developer of the game that went viral, I formally apologize to the Steam store.” It's funny, but also a bit bleak. One comment called it the 'Robloxification of Steam.'
Just as Roblox is flooded with clones of trending titles like 'Mecha Chameleon,' Steam now seems to be swimming in imitators too.

A quick search turns up plenty of Needle in a Haystack clones, and many of them show clear signs of leaning on generative AI to some degree. That's the final touch. It doesn't look good for Valve's platform, but it's also not easy to control.

Whenever something takes off, it shows up everywhere. The problem comes when it crowds out the real original or outright steals the idea. Many of these clones look closer to the latter. Whether the imitators get taken down remains to be seen. The original is coming out later this year.

Did you know that Reaper, the ground enemy you meet in ARC Raiders, learns its behavior through machine learning? Embark Studios' machine learning research lead, Martin Singh-Blom, explained at this year's GDC that Reaper learns through reward and perception. As a result, Reaper moves naturally and can adapt on its own even when it loses a leg.

It's not quite accurate to call it AI-driven, but there's clearly a resemblance. Reaper isn't the only enemy that uses this approach, but its long legs and movement make it the most noticeable. With the Frozen Trail update, the biggest yet, arriving October 8, another enemy with the same machine learning ability joins the game. Its name is Bully.

True to its name, Bully is aggressive and powerful. Polygon saw Bully in motion at an online press and creator briefing held before the Frozen Trail reveal. It isn't as large as Reaper, but it's a very sturdily built ground enemy. It chases players relentlessly, giving them no room to breathe. Like Reaper, the goal is for it to stumble, fall, and crash into players mid-fight to create dynamic moments.

Executive producer Alexander Grondahl said, “Machine learning is still a nascent technology, and for us it remains close to an advanced research topic. What's interesting is that you can't control it that precisely. Even when you try to teach a behavior, it sometimes moves in a way that makes no sense at all, and we have to update the model to fix a specific issue.”

He explained that the machine learning enemies “fill an archetypal role within the roster.” “As the technology improves and we learn more, we'll use it in the best possible way to create a unique experience.”

Of Bully, he said, “It's a ground enemy, so it tries to get over any terrain.” “All the machine learning enemies move based on physics, and thanks to the new tether system, players can play with these enemies' physicality in a whole new way. Machine learning enemies work best when they have legs to learn to walk with. It's fun to see how they adapt when they lose a leg, get stuck, or fall and roll.”
Frozen Trail arrives as a free update on Thursday, October 8, for PS5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X.
If you use a console long enough, you eventually run into a technical bug that needs fixing. Sony wants to sidestep that problem with an AI tech support agent.

In Sony's patent, the AI watches the system and writes a patch using an LLM when it detects something unusual. The patch can fix the problem in advance or send a report to a Sony engineer. The catch is that, if the feature can't be turned off, all the data processed on the PlayStation could be visible to this agent. Monitoring every hardware and software issue without exception would essentially require full access.

There's also a risk of making a small problem worse. The patent language found by Patently also states that “an automated system that sends repair instructions to a device in the living room needs careful guardrails so that small problems don't spiral into bigger ones.” The PS5 (and likely the PS6) is, in the end, just a specialized computer. The author has more than once broken something while trying to fix a small problem that could have been left alone.
If the LLM's training and guardrails aren't solid enough, a mistake in an improvised patch could brick a PlayStation.

It's unclear when, or even whether, this patent will become an actual AI tech support agent. Still, once the PS6 drops the disc drive, the next-generation console will likely require an always-on internet connection from the start. If it's always communicating with Sony's servers, adding a system like this wouldn't be hard. The author expects this feature to first appear on the next-generation platform. Until then, let's hope there's time to work out the operational and privacy issues that come with remote AI monitoring.

Niikawa Sohei, creator of Disgaea, served as president of Nippon Ichi Software and is now CEO of SuperNICHI. In a recent Dengeki Online interview, he discussed the use of generative AI in game development.

Niikawa sees AI not as a threat but as a “tool.” He's fine with using it to boost productivity, but firmly opposes illegal uses such as copyright infringement. For now, he doesn't plan to use AI in his own work, and even less so for writing.

“You could put together just the plot, feed it to AI, and let it handle the rest of the story. I'm sure a lot of people are already doing that. I have no intention of denying that approach. I just wonder whether it would really be fun.”

AI may be a good tool for mass production, but churning out games en masse isn't his goal. “I have a fundamental desire to create the stories and characters I want to see. It's no fun unless I shape each one with my own hands. I don't enjoy it unless I thread together every single word myself.”

This is the biggest reason he doesn't use AI for creative work. It might be useful for naming characters or looking up information, but he said, “I have absolutely no interest in having AI write a story in my place.” “I don't even want to ask AI for ten story ideas that would sell well. I find value in picking the subjects I find interesting myself and writing them myself.”

Niikawa is currently handling the scenario and production for several new titles, including the speedrun-training SRPG Demons' Night Fever and the time-loop horror stealth-action adventure Noroi Ayashi: The ∞th Oddity. The concepts and scenarios are entirely human-made. Demons' Night Fever is set to launch on October 22, 2026, for PC (Steam), PS5, and Nintendo Switch, while Noroi Ayashi is slated for 2027 on PC (Steam), Nintendo Switch, and Switch 2.

Have you ever watched an Argentine horror film? I have, and it's genuinely frightening. The mini-documentary at PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct 2026 had to be watched with one hand covering my eyes. Tenebris Somnia mixes 2D survival horror gameplay with live-action cutscenes shot by an award-winning Argentine film crew. The makeup and special effects are good enough to be scary.

The retro 2D visuals and live-action cutscenes mesh together skillfully. You'll walk down an eerie, colorful corridor one moment, and the next you'll see a real person's face twist in ways that defy logic. Publisher New Blood Interactive CEO Dave Oshry praises the special effects team, but I wonder if they cast an actual demon.

Executive producer Airdorf said it feels like playing inside someone's nightmare. There's a monster with another face beneath its face, and another connected by a single mouth. Most of these effects were made with physical materials, which is why they feel so convincing. Oshry said, “Let's just say AI could never make Tenebris Somnia.”

The survival side is also worth looking forward to. “You'll always have just enough health. You'll always have just enough ammo, too. There will be plenty of times you'll have to rely on a wrench or a pipe.” Oshry explains this in the video while holding a wrench.

The story is said to resonate with anyone who has been through a difficult relationship. “You'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll call your ex.” That's the scariest thing revealed so far. Tenebris Somnia launches on October 16, 2026, in time for Halloween.

Starform released Metal Storm in November 2023. When the Seattle studio raised $6 million from Bitkraft in late 2024, the 5v5 aerial combat game had 3 million players combined across the App Store, Google Play, and the Epic Games Store. Lou Pasculli, CEO and co-founder, now puts that number at 15 million. PocketGamer.biz met with him at SLICE 2026.

Pasculli doesn't inflate the label the studio gave itself. “AI-native is more of a journey than a state. I wouldn't say AI let us do things we couldn't do before.” What changed is throughput. “We've shipped a lot more features, and incorporated a lot more player feedback. The play experience ended up better.” Internally, the team thinks of one end as rote, repetitive work and the other end as judgment. The longer team members stay on the judgment and creativity side, the more ambition a small team can have.

He's also clear about the limits. Looking at demos that make a whole game from a single prompt, he counted the decisions that go into a single Metal Storm fighter craft: things like the acceleration curve, how much energy bleeds off in a hard turn, and how readable its silhouette is at 800 meters. Across the whole game, he figures that adds up to tens of thousands. “If you don't decide even one of them, the model just invents it. That's fine for a prototype.”

On team size, he says “the right size for the game and the right size for the company are probably different,” using culture and a shared vision as the measure. “If the team grows so large that it can't absorb feedback from the 2,100 people who took part in the last Halo update, one person's voice and contribution shrink to almost nothing.” A bigger team also raises the break-even point. “I think of double-A as a cost structure, not a destination.”

When new-player reactions were sharply divided over an early Metal Storm build with heavy simulation elements, Starform overhauled every mechanic instead of making a 10% improvement. Pasculli says the studio isn't currently raising investment, adding, “It's not us who keeps the game alive, it's the players who love the game.” He points to a shift in where the expensive part sits as the reason 26 people can run Metal Storm and plan the next title at the same time. “The discovery and R&D we call gameplay innovation isn't expensive. What's expensive is scaling up production enough to carry it all the way through and deliver it to players.”

blocks.x: Ubisoft internally calls its latest generative AI venture 'Motherbrain.' Yes, the same name as the evil supercomputer-turned-grotesque brain-in-a-jar from Nintendo's Metroid series. The fact comes from a trademark filing by the maker of Assassin's Creed and Far Cry.
The Game File first reported it, and Kotaku picked it up. Several recent trademark filings use this ominous name to refer to the company's various generative AI plans.

According to the report, one trademark covers 'downloadable computer software that uses artificial intelligence (AI) for creating video games and interactive content.' Another covers AI services used for both 'data analysis and interacting with humans,' as well as research and design of 'software utilizing artificial intelligence.'

Ubisoft has not yet mentioned Motherbrain publicly. For now it appears to be an internal-only name. Still, the company has long been openly enthusiastic about this controversial technology and its use in game development.

In 2023 it released a generative AI ghostwriting tool meant to help write background dialogue for NPCs — fittingly named Ghostwriter. Late last year, CEO Yves Guillemot said generative AI had been adopted across the whole company, calling it a 'revolution' on par with the shift from 2D to 3D. This summer the company said it would 'accelerate' investment in Teammates, described as Ubisoft's 'first playable generative AI experience' shooter.
Whether this plan will someday turn into a pointy-headed, one-eyed brain remains to be seen.

In January this year, Ubisoft closed two studios, canceled six projects and laid off developers in what was called a major restructuring. A few months earlier, it closed two more studios and reorganized another, cutting roughly 380 jobs.
Nintendo Wii classic Super Mario Galaxy has been 100% decompiled. Game community members say an unofficial PC port is coming soon.

Game decompilation has been one of the big trends in 2020s PC gaming. Porting games that never came out on PC lets them run natively and even be improved, which is far more useful than just using an emulator. Thanks to this, PC players finally got to enjoy classics like Castlevania: Symphony of the Night and Blue Dragon.

Unfortunately, as with many things these days, generative AI is muddying this scene too. Vibe-coding attempts keep piling up, from Donkey Kong 64 to Mario Kart Wii to, much to this writer's disappointment, Monster Hunter Portable 3rd. Emulators aren't exempt either. The developers behind RPCS3, the best-known PS3 emulator, pleaded with contributors to “stop sending AI slop code.” It's no wonder suspicion is the first reaction to every new project. Fortunately, this new project — also a Wii Mario game — proudly flies the flag of '100% human-written code.'

Modding community Luma's Workshop announced in a video titled 'the next step…' that the Super Mario Galaxy decompilation had reached nearly 100%. According to a comment update, it hit 100% six hours later. The group also shared news of the PC port, named Astrocore, and even showed it running. The developers said they “expect to release it soon” and pointed to Discord for updates.

There was also word on a follow-up. The developers said “the Luma's Workshop decompilation team will move on to Super Mario Galaxy 2 once cleanup work is finished.” A PC port of the (perhaps better) sequel may not be far off either.

Unofficial as it is, this implementation now lets unsupported hardware hit 60FPS with DLSS 5. Developer Daniel has been picking up the pace on improving AMD hardware performance lately. Just days ago, running the latest demanding games smoothly with DLSS 5 was nearly impossible — but he pulled it off.

Two days ago came news that he had boosted performance by nearly 74% in a single day. That wasn't the end of it. Over the following two days he put out several major updates to the DLSS-NR-on-AMD runtime tool. Alpha 0.4.0 raised performance about 42%, and the following Alpha 0.4.1 was 8% faster than 0.4.0.

blocks.cap: Alpha 0.4.1 release notes: 8% improvement over 0.4.0

blocks.x: A new priority queue mode added another 9% in heavy gameplay sections. Alpha 0.4.2, released yesterday, added 15% over 0.4.1 — an improvement for the Fast mode used by the RX 9000 series. Fast mode is now the default on Radeon RX 9000 GPUs and uses less costly arithmetic operations.

blocks.cap: Alpha 0.4.2 release notes: 15% improvement over 0.4.1 in Fast mode
Alpha 0.4.3 release notes: 20% improvement over 0.4.2, 75FPS in Cyberpunk at 1080p

blocks.x: According to the developer, even though Fast mode gives the GPU less work to do, the image quality difference from Reference mode is still hard to spot. Radeon RX 7000 still defaults to Reference mode. A few hours ago came another major update, Alpha 0.4.3 — a big one, nearly 20% faster than 0.4.2 in Reference mode and about 18% faster in Fast mode.

Across the three most recent releases, Radeon GPU performance improved by 46-49% overall. As a result, the Radeon RX 9070 XT runs Cyberpunk 2077 at 1080p, DLSS 5 Fast mode, at 75FPS — a GPU that used to struggle even at 30FPS. With performance up more than 200% in just days, the latest games with DLSS 5 turned on are now plenty playable on AMD hardware.

More platforms are rolling out generative AI disclosure rules, but Twitch CEO Dan Clancy doesn't think the live-streaming platform needs to rush to follow suit. He shared the view in an interview with GamesBeat at Tokyo Game Show 2026, where he gave a keynote on September 17. He acknowledged that disclosure rules matter for other platforms, but said the behavior that prompted those rules is still far from common on Twitch.

“If that happens, we'll obviously take similar steps. On YouTube there's no way to know whether a video is AI or not, so it matters to users to know what's real.” That's Clancy's view. “If it became common for streamers to put up an AI in their place, to the point where people start wondering, ‘Is this really that streamer?’ — of course we'd have to. But that's not happening.”

AI disclosure policies have spread quickly over the past year. YouTube, TikTok and Instagram require labeling or disclosure when realistic AI video or audio is used. Valve requires disclosure of generative AI use before launching on Steam, and refined its policy in January 2026 to cover both in-game content and store page promotional material. Live-streaming platform Kick also added strict disclosure requirements for AI-generated content to its community guidelines in March 2026.

Clancy is an AI expert who holds a doctorate in artificial intelligence from the University of Texas at Austin. Generative AI's presence on Twitch has also grown over the past year. Last month, creators noticed that a feature allowing their content to be used to train Amazon's generative AI models was opted in by default.

“We've always used AI. Automod, one of Twitch's foundations, already used AI back in 2013. We have a responsibility to use AI to make the product better, by continuing to improve moderation and recommendations. What a lot of people are probably curious about is the AI that shows up on-stream.”

He said generative AI is also used in Twitch broadcasts, but most viewers can easily spot it. As an example, he pointed to well-known streamer team “Esfand” Esfandiari. Esfand made heavy use of videos made with Sora 2 in some content, asking viewers to make videos of him doing funny things and then watching and ranking them together on-stream. Clancy said “AI actually boosted the community's creativity,” adding that “it was made together with the community, not a replacement in any sense.”

Clancy made clear he has both the will and the capacity to introduce a generative AI disclosure policy whenever he judges it necessary. But he's skeptical that a policy drafted in advance would properly account for the circumstances unique to live creators. “Writing policy for a hypothetical situation is always hard. In practice, the policy ends up being wrong, because whatever actually happens will differ from what I assumed.”

blocks.cap: The best console version of Final Fantasy VII Revelation looks set to be the PS5 Pro edition

blocks.x: If there's one feature that sets the PS5 Pro apart from the base model, it's the PSSR (PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution) upscaler, alongside enhanced ray tracing. It's Sony's machine-learning-based upscaling technology, the main driver pushing the limits of this generation's console games. Thanks to PSSR's improved new version from earlier this year, the PS5 Pro looks set to be the answer for enjoying Final Fantasy VII Revelation at 4K resolution and 60 frames per second.

“On PS5 Pro, we've implemented a mode that delivers both 4K visuals and 60FPS gameplay using PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR).” That's what series director Naoki Hamaguchi confirmed on X. “For those who want both better visuals and smooth performance, the PS5 Pro will be one of the recommended ways to enjoy REVELATION.”

This kind of enthusiastic talk about a particular game's PS5 Pro version has come up many times over the past few years. In many cases it didn't really hold up, since there was little improvement over the base PS5 version. Still, there's good reason to believe Hamaguchi's words.

I played Final Fantasy VII Revelation's open-world demo myself at Gamescom, and it did run on an actual PS5 Pro. I mostly play games on PC, so I rarely find myself impressed by a console version. But I clearly remember being struck by this demo's clean visuals, high resolution and smooth performance. It dipped below 60FPS here and there, but that's understandable with the game still months from release. Overall, the technical polish was impressive.
For context, I was playing — and still am — Final Fantasy VII Rebirth on PC with mods like Shader Injector at the time. If there had been a big technical gap, I would have noticed it immediately.

With GTA 6 also promising its best experience on this device from launch, the PS5 Pro is becoming an increasingly appealing option for anyone who wants to properly enjoy console gaming. Purely on technical terms, a high-end PC that can run mods is still the best choice. Recent price hikes have raised the barrier compared to launch, but Sony's mid-generation refresh model should keep pulling its weight going forward.

Meta unveiled two AI game-making tools at its Connect event: Horizon Create, for mobile, and Horizon Studio, for browsers. Both run on the agentic creation features of the Meta Horizon Engine and share a backend, so assets, systems, and edit history carry over between the two tools.

Using them is simple. Describe the game you want in a text prompt, and the Horizon Engine builds a playable game that can be posted directly to Facebook and Instagram. Meta said that “traditional game development requires months of work, expensive equipment, and specialized skills,” and that the two tools make it “easier to turn ideas into playable 2D and 3D games.”

According to MobileGamerBiz, some creators backed by the Meta Horizon Creator Fund are currently testing the app. Early access will roll out in stages, and in-game monetization details will be announced later. Earlier this year, Roblox also added an agentic AI feature to Roblox Studio that turns text prompts into game design documents and then implements and tests them directly.

VR glasses were also announced at the event. They are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 and feature a micro-OLED-based 5K display. Unity 6.6 supports them via OpenXR from day one, letting existing Quest projects be ported over. They launch in spring 2027 at $1,299.99.

WeAreMighty has stopped developing games and renamed itself Secretsauce Labs. Going forward, it will focus solely on AI content technology for brands. Its predecessor, Mighty Bear Games, made Disney Melee Mania and Butter Royal and had renamed itself WeAreMighty in January 2026.

It started as a headache on the production floor. In late 2022, CEO Simon Davis and co-founder Ben were building a game that needed roughly 25 million brand-matched avatars. Doing it by hand was impossible, and the generative AI of the time produced inconsistent results. Davis recalled, “Ask for the same character twice and the face or clothes would change, and sometimes you'd get an extra finger.” The team then spent the next three years building the infrastructure needed to use AI output in an actual production pipeline.

He says the core issue is brand consistency. “Plenty of tools let you upload a logo, past assets, and a style guide. What's still unsolved is checking every newly generated output against that material one by one, catching mismatches before a human sees them,” he said. Of scale, brand, and cost, brand drift was by far the hardest, he said, because cost is a budgeting problem while brand drift is a research problem.

He also pushes back on the idea that “AI saves time.” If you generate 10 assets and can only use 2, that isn't fast. Under the right conditions, a six-person art team's three-month job can be finished by one person in a day — but only when the output can be used immediately. He also criticized much of what generative AI game tools call “creative control” as mostly “theater.” Davis said, “What's hard isn't generation, it's memory and judgment,” adding, “We're not reselling inference, we're selling results.”

ONE Store has opened its AI game section, “AI Games,” which it unveiled last August, to all developers. Its developer center, ONEconsole, has begun accepting AI-based game registrations. In early October, the section will be renamed “AI Game” and added to the app's bottom menu.

The idea is to connect individual and small developers who use generative AI with a distribution channel and users. Developers without coding experience or a separate development team can register a game as long as it was made through conversation with AI. When listing a product on ONEconsole, marking it as an AI-made game makes it eligible for the “AI Game” menu. ONE Store plans to introduce the most polished registered games to users first.
It will first support web games (HTML5) that can be played without installation. Adding the ONE Store web game SDK enables revenue through in-app purchases and in-app ads.

The revamped “AI Game” menu, launching in early October, will stay fixed at the bottom of the app so it can be reached from any screen with one tap. It will feature both games from Buseight, which has taken part in curation since last August, and works developers upload themselves.

ONE Store CEO Chang Hyun-kook said, “The rapid advance of AI models is accelerating a paradigm shift in which high-quality, fun AI games are pouring out at tremendous speed,” adding, “ONE Store will actively embrace this change and become the mobile distribution platform for AI games.” ONE Store plans to launch the service domestically first, then expand AI game availability worldwide.

Com2uS Platform introduced its next-generation backend platform, Hive Axyl, at an AI game development event in Tokyo, Japan. It launches officially on September 30 and handles everything from game backend setup and feature integration to live operations.

Com2uS Platform, a subsidiary of Com2uS Holdings, unveiled Hive Axyl on the 28th at the finals of the “Tokyo AI (TAI) | OpenAI: 100-Hour Game Builder Challenge.” In the challenge, hosted by Tokyo AI (TAI) and supported by OpenAI, participating teams used OpenAI Codex to build AI-native games and AI tools for game-making over 100 hours.

Speaking at the finals, Com2uS Japan CEO Kim Jin-yong presented the vision “Build with Codex, Play with Hive.” He also shared the experience of “OpenAI Game Builders Seoul,” an event Com2uS and OpenAI co-hosted in Seoul in August. Attendees included figures from the Korean and Japanese IT industries, including Krit Ventures and LY Corporation.

CEO Kim explained that Hive Axyl “gives developers an environment where they can focus on content creation instead of complex backend work.” He also said he hopes Hive Axyl will help when the games built that day are launched.

Built for AI game development, Hive Axyl supports Codex plugin integration. Natural-language prompts can quickly connect key functions such as backend setup, authentication, payments, data analytics, and live operations. After the official launch, developers can install the plugin by following the guide on the developer site.

In 43 minutes: 11,138 reasoning tokens, six commands, zero combat units. That is the report card Grok 4.6 earned in 'StarCraft: Brood War' after its reasoning intensity was set to the highest level (xhigh). On the other end of the same leaderboard, GPT-6's Astra went 18-0, a 100% win rate. The 'Brood War Bench' leaderboard recently became a topic on Hacker News.

blocks.cap: The Brood War Bench top 10. Astra, at the highest reasoning level, went 18-0.

blocks.x: Developer Ben Swardlow first built a version of StarCraft where an agent handled all the controls, and played it with friends for fun. Even friends who had barely played StarCraft before could type a single command like 'attack' and watch the AI handle production, rallying and combat like a veteran. So what happens if humans step away entirely? 19 AI players from the GPT, Claude and Grok families gathered and played a total of 171 matches.

A real-time strategy game does not wait for a model to finish thinking. In match G043, Grok issued only six commands in 43 minutes, roughly one every seven minutes, and at its highest reasoning level it finished 2 wins and 15 losses, sitting on ample resources it never used. Astra, by contrast, won with harassment, sending a single worker into enemy territory to leave the opposing AI stuck thinking for tens of seconds at a time.

blocks.cap: Astra's worker and zealot tore through Grok's base. Grok had stockpiled 928 minerals without a single combat unit.

blocks.x: Fable played the most human-like game, building its economy and tech steadily to finish third with an 83.3% win rate, though in one match it over-invested in tech and collapsed against Claude Opus 5. Cost is worth noting too: Astra made 12.6 actions per minute and spent $10.54 per match at its highest reasoning level, versus 25.7 actions per minute and $21.07 at its lowest. It made fewer moves, spent less and still won the most.

Still, Swardlow's verdict is sober: even Astra, the undefeated champion, cannot beat a human beginner. That stands in contrast to 2019, when DeepMind's AlphaStar beat professional players TLO and MaNa 5-0 on 2 separate occasions and climbed to Grandmaster, the top 0.2% of the European ladder.

blocks.cap: UE Box chat screen: question, tool call, answer

blocks.x: An open-source AI agent called UE Box (虚幻盒子) appeared on the Epic Developer Community forum. Its developer said the tool does not just talk about code — it works directly inside the Unreal Editor.

Given a goal, it places actors, fixes Blueprints, and wires up materials. When a C++ compile error occurs, it fixes the error and reruns the build. It pauses for approval at risky steps, and each round leaves a change log you can check against the editor state.

The UnrealAgentLink plugin gives it access to more than 100 engine tools, and 25 built-in skills cover common UE tasks. It is not built only for the latest MCP setups — it supports UE 5.0 through 5.8. It runs locally without an account, and the API key stays only on the user's PC. The app is licensed under Apache-2.0, and the plugin under MIT.

An English-language site and a GitHub repository (ueboxai/uebox) are open, and a Windows installer is available. The developer asked for blunt feedback on places where the agent's edits feel unstable, and where Blueprint or material graphs still break.

Spiral AI, developer of the chatbot RPG 'RyzaChat:AI' based on Atelier Ryza, said it will restrict user input starting with its October AI model update. The move follows concerns that some players' abuse could damage the reputation of the Atelier series and its characters.

Spiral AI reissued its terms of service, saying it would not tolerate acts that “disparage the original work or undermine its integrity.” This covers attempts to make Ryza's character AI say things that violate public order and morals, and manipulated or faked screenshots that distort the game's content.

The game already has a three-stage monitoring system. Input first goes to a game-master AI, which breaks down the content and filters out inappropriate words before passing it to the character AI. Ryza's character AI is built not to respond to topics unrelated to the character or the game's setting, and immediately deletes any inappropriate expression in a generated response. Inappropriate content is also not stored in the character AI's memory.

Still, users got past the filters using methods such as prompt injection. Starting with the October update, the content users can enter while talking with Ryza will be restricted. The company plans to keep watching the situation while also considering additional measures such as character limits.

Spiral AI has begun filing takedown requests and reports with each platform over manipulated screenshots that distort the game. Given how much it values character integrity, the same restriction is likely to extend to the upcoming 'SophieChat: AI,' featuring Sophie Neuenmuller, the protagonist of Atelier Sophie. RyzaChat:AI is available on iOS and Android.

Tsuda Kenjiro, a veteran voice actor known for roles in popular anime such as Jujutsu Kaisen and Chainsaw Man, lost a lawsuit against TikTok. The suit sought removal of videos that used generative AI to mimic his voice. According to a Nikkei report, the Tokyo District Court dismissed the claim on September 30 because the videos had already been removed from the platform. Still, the ruling set an important precedent for how Japan will legally protect the voices of voice actors and celebrities.

Filed in November 2025 and made public in May this year, the suit sought the immediate removal of about 180 videos from an anonymous individual account with more than 210,000 followers. The videos used AI narration in a voice very similar to Tsuda's to tell trivia and urban-legend stories, and generated roughly $3,000 to $4,700 a month in revenue.

Tsuda's side argued the videos made viewers mistake the AI voice for his own, and claimed violations of Japan's Unfair Competition Prevention Act and infringement of publicity rights — rights that protect the commercial value of a celebrity's identity.

TikTok countered that the narration was an “ordinary male voice” and that the uploader used “AI trained on a friend's voice” from an outside site. It argued there was no violation of the law or infringement of Tsuda's rights. The account had already been deleted in May, and no data remained on TikTok's servers. The defense asked for dismissal, saying there was no legal interest in continuing the suit.

The court dismissed the claim because the videos had been removed. Even so, it stated in the ruling that a person's voice is subject to protection under publicity rights, and Japanese media have called this a new precedent.

Unauthorized use of celebrities' voices and likenesses through generative AI has continued in recent years, but Japan has no law that directly protects voice rights. As the issue has grown, voice-actor groups and others have strongly pushed for legal reform. The Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry have issued draft guidance saying a voice, like a likeness, could be protected under publicity rights and the Unfair Competition Prevention Act, but until now no ruling had recognized a violation of voice rights — which is why this ruling carries weight.

Over the past week, the Steam app Borderless Gaming added two features: frame generation and DLSS 5 neural rendering. According to developer Andrew Sampson (creator of the streaming tech Rainway), frame generation is a general-purpose implementation trained on “tens of thousands of hours of gameplay,” so it does not need to touch the game. The DLSS 5 effect also uses the BGFX mode introduced earlier this year, which captures the game window at the compositor stage and processes it through a GPU effects pipeline.

Unlike existing injection tools, it does not require swapping game DLLs, patching files, or hunting for game-specific mods. You install the effect, pick a preset, and apply it to a running game — that's it. This works because it never calls NVIDIA's software at all. Sampson said he quantized the model, restructured how it runs, and removed internal bottlenecks in the neural network so it runs on a much wider range of GPUs than the latest GeForce RTX cards. NVIDIA officially supports only the RTX 50 series, but this version can target around 30FPS on an RTX 3090 depending on the game and settings.

blocks.cap: Borderless Gaming DLSS 5 effect comparison

blocks.x: Sampson stressed that the DLSS 5 effect is not bundled with the update, and does not turn on by default or run in the background. The effect is a single shader file hosted on GitHub, and this update added the ability to paste a repository URL to install effects and presets. Once installed, you can adjust intensity, lighting, structure, style, and processing resolution.

Wccftech noted that since the model itself was modified and it processes a captured compositor-stage image, it would be more accurate to call this a “DLSS 5 derivative” rather than NVIDIA's 3D-guided neural rendering itself. Still, it observed that amid the controversy, the continuing attempts to attach this technology to games and other tools outside of games show the appeal of DLSS 5.

blocks.cap: Logitech G Hub Replay screen

blocks.x: Jacob at PC Gamer first saw Logitech's new software Replay last week in Warsaw. It's currently in beta. Record your games, and deep learning finds the good moments and stitches them together. The demo looked convincing, but trying it himself in Counter-Strike 2 showed it still has a way to go.

After recording one CS2 deathmatch and half of a casual match, the result had no standout moments. A few kills made it in, but nothing impressive. In the deathmatch especially, only a couple of clips were picked, while later moments like a deagle kill, a Scout quickscope, and a flick no-scope were left out. So he recorded one deathmatch separately to compare the AI-picked clips again.

blocks.cap: Replay clip editing screen

blocks.x: Fortunately, you can pick and fix scenes directly from the full recording. Spending about five minutes editing the same match recording produced a much better video. This is based on just one CS2 game, and not a deep dive. Logitech currently lists 44 compatible games, and the software can be downloaded and tried for free.

Aside from the core AI clip-selection feature, the software itself is fairly solid. It starts recording automatically with a small popup when you launch a game, and once you quit the game you can freely edit by adding and removing clips. You can also set a storage cap, and once it's reached, the oldest recordings get deleted first. He noticed no performance drop while recording, but that was on a high-end PC, so results may vary depending on the setup.
PSSR은 PS5 Pro에 AI 업스케일링을 가져왔지만, GPU 성능이 낮은 기본 PS5는 그 혜택을 받지 못했다. Sony는 블로그 글에서 기본 콘솔에서 돌아가는 새 모델 Quick Spectral Super Resolution, 즉 QSSR을 자세히 소개했다. PSSR처럼 AMD와 함께한 Project Amethyst 협업에서 나왔다.
QSSR은 PSSR보다 훨씬 가벼워서 PS5 Pro의 PSSR만큼 디테일을 살리지는 못한다. 그래도 이 콘솔이 전통적으로 쓰던 템포럴 업스케일링보다는 훨씬 정확할 것으로 보인다.

QSSR은 Marvel's Wolverine과 Ghost of Yotei에서 처음 적용된다. Insomniac의 Mike Fitzgerald는 QSSR이 "PS5 플레이어에게 PS5 Pro 경험을 제대로 맛보게 해 준다"고 말했다. Sony 비교 영상에서 QSSR은 먼 건물과 수풀의 세밀한 디테일을 훨씬 더 많이 살린다. 다만 화면이 여전히 흐릿하거나 노이즈가 조금 낄 때도 있다.
Sony는 QSSR을 모든 개발사에 제공한다고 밝혔다. 두 게임의 패치는 오늘 나온다.

Patrice Désilets reaffirmed that he has removed all AI-made assets from 1666: Amsterdam, and won't use them going forward. He apologized for the parts that slipped through unfiltered, and said it won't happen again.

blocks.cap: Image: GamesRadar+

blocks.x: "We live in a world full of AI. Between us, that's the honest truth." That's Désilets's statement. "But there were parts of the pipeline we didn't clean up enough. Since then, we've made sure not to use AI anywhere in the game."

The controversy began after this witch action-adventure was revealed at Summer Game Fest. Sharp-eyed players spotted AI-generated artwork in a short free demo Panache Digital posted on Steam. The Assassin's Creed creator told reporters at a recent hands-on event that it "won't be in the final product." As soon as the generative AI art was flagged, he put an illustrator on cleaning it up, and now says every image is "real."

According to Désilets, the team used AI tools early in development. "I can ask AI to turn one thing into 75 variations. I can't call in 75 illustrators and get variations back in 3 seconds. That's the world we live in, and we're a small team making this game," he said. "Eventually, we didn't even notice it was AI anymore, because we got used to looking at it."
"I'm really sorry about that. Honestly, it's something we did among ourselves 2 to 3 years ago. Something slipped through unfiltered when we put the demo out. It won't happen again."
1666: Amsterdam enters Early Access on August 25. It can be downloaded and played on PC via Steam.
Fenris Creations (formerly CCP Games), the studio behind EVE Online, has hired former Icelandic minister Áslaug Arna Sigurbjörnsdóttir as director of AI partnerships.

Sigurbjörnsdóttir served as Iceland's minister of justice and minister of higher education, science and innovation. Fenris has put her in charge of working with AI labs, universities, policymakers, and strategic partners. It's a new research initiative set against EVE Frontier, EVE Online's survival spinoff.

blocks.cap: An EVE Frontier ship crossing a red sci-fi horizon

blocks.x: The company's announcement read: "Fenris Creations has spent the past few months preparing to test a bold hypothesis—that a persistent virtual world backed by real social and economic systems, like EVE Frontier, could serve as a living stage to test advanced AI before it becomes more deeply embedded in our daily lives."

"Instead of relying only on short simulations that reset when they end, the goal is to create a place where autonomous agents can be observed alongside real people, inside an open, evolving economy with real consequences—within the kind of dynamic system only the company's game can offer."

The Reykjavik-based studio sees the EVE universe as well suited to training autonomous AI, since it has no fixed endpoint and is an unpredictable universe shaped by the choices of hundreds of thousands of people.

"That makes this one of the few places where you can study the behavior of autonomous systems under conditions close to a real society, a real economy—including the irrational, emotional, and unpredictable responses that real people bring," the company explained.

"In EVE Frontier, the new chapter of the EVE universe, autonomous AI systems set goals, respond to change, and sustain consistent decisions over long stretches of time. That process is observed within a living, open world. Researchers can better evaluate model behavior in genuinely complex environments and draw on it to develop future AI responsibly."

Fenris says this research will also improve EVE Frontier itself, used to make NPC behavior richer and refine the onboarding process for new players. "If the plan succeeds, it opens up an entirely new role for Fenris Creations and EVE Frontier—making a meaningful contribution to research on intelligent agents, complex systems, and AI alignment, while also expanding the range of experiences EVE Frontier can offer players."
Sigurbjörnsdóttir said her experience making and enforcing policy will help the studio and its partners—making "meaningful progress" with the regulators overseeing the AI sector.

"There is no bigger opportunity to help shape the future of AI innovation together—being part of a testbed that helps our partners make meaningful progress with regulators and build safe, practical, and trustworthy AI standards," she said. "I'll help Fenris push this work forward responsibly."
The news comes a few months after Fenris announced it would stand as an independent studio and entered a research partnership with Google DeepMind, at which point Google took a stake in the studio.

Around when No Man's Sky first came out, its biggest boast was its sophisticated algorithms. They generated more planets than a single person could visit even living a billion lifetimes. Ten years later, some companies promise that another technology, large language models and generative AI, can inflate a developer's output just as far beyond imagination. Hello Games CEO Sean Murray says he has no plans to join that race.

blocks.cap: No Man's Sky

blocks.x: "I remember coming back from COVID. Everyone was figuring out how to run studios and game companies." He said this in an interview with Kotaku for No Man's Sky's 10th anniversary. "How do you get people working together again? Call them back to the office? Go hybrid? We talked about that a lot. I remember saying at the time, 'Let's hold back a bit. Keep working from home, and let everyone else screw it up first.'"

Despite all the claims and fears around generative AI, Murray plans to respond the same way. Before co-founding Hello Games, he was at Criterion Games. In 2006, while he was lead programmer on the cult FPS Black, the company was owned by Electronic Arts. EA is reported to be covering some of the debt from its $55 billion sale to Saudi Arabia with new AI technology.

"I read the article about EA being sold to the Saudis," he said. "It's like, 'Don't worry, we're going to use AI for everything, so we'll save billions of dollars.' That kind of thing. And I just sit there and think, great, good luck, let's see how that goes. I'll watch from a distance."

Just as Murray waited to see how office work settled after COVID, he plans to watch what becomes the industry standard over the next few years. Just a few months ago, major games from the Tomb Raider remake to the new Crazy Taxi faced fan backlash after revealing they'd used some generative AI in development. Players worry slop will end up in the finished game, and developers haven't clearly explained what adding the technology actually improves.

Murray's prediction is this: AI won't change the fundamental difficulty of making a good game. "Making games is really hard, and people are going to learn that hard things are still hard—making something feel good to play," he added. "My day-to-day role is just to enjoy making games the way we always have. That still works for us, and we still enjoy it."

Axolotl3D is a unified model that generates 3D shapes from incomplete observations arriving in different forms. Whether it's reconstructing from photos, filling in occluded parts, or touching up a shape that already exists, one model handles all of it.

Recent 3D generation methods have improved a lot in quality, but they assume an ideal condition: a clean single image showing the whole object. Reality is different. Objects are partly occluded, captured from only a handful of viewpoints, or survive only as partial 3D data. Sometimes you also want to fix a flaw in a shape you've already built, or change just one part of it.

Researchers have been solving these problems one at a time. Each approach was strong in its own domain, but nothing spanned all four. The starting point for Axolotl3D is the observation that all four tasks ultimately come down to completing a 3D object from incomplete observations.

Whatever forms of input come in, each is encoded and merged into multimodal conditioning tokens. These tokens condition a diffusion transformer to produce a completed shape latent. The key is how it's trained: it simulates varied partial observations across a large 3D dataset and mixes inputs on the fly. That makes cross-modality reasoning robust and lets it carry over to many situations.

This shows up in a real image-to-3D pipeline too. A handful of photos are used to predict and align camera and 3D points, which are then handed to the model to produce the final mesh. In effect, a complete 3D mesh comes out of casually taken photos.

Local editing works too. Paint directly over a rendered view to mark where to edit, an inpainting model generates the changed appearance, and Axolotl3D lifts that into 3D geometry. Because the original point cloud is kept as a condition, the untouched areas stay exactly as they were.

It can also pull an incomplete object straight out of a real captured scene. Once a user segments an object in the scene, its splats become the conditioning points, and the model produces a mesh that's ready to use in simulation. Unlike a Gaussian splat fragment that's left with large holes, a completed mesh makes physics simulation far more accurate.

The authors also noted a limitation: because the model follows input points faithfully, how well it holds up against noisy input is left as a balance to work out going forward. The research has been accepted to ECCV 2026, and the authors are Anita Hu and Maria Shugrina.

Teaching parkour to a virtual human is a strange problem. Knowing every move perfectly is useless if you don't know when to use which one. A perfect jump means nothing if the vaulting box has shifted out of reach.

Systems that strictly imitate a human look beautiful, but they're brittle and repetitive. Systems that chase a goal adapt well, but they often stop moving like a human. This research sets out to do both: it remembers human motion precisely while still knowing when to break from the script if it has to.

The training data is surprisingly small: 19 parkour videos pulled from the internet, 30 seconds in total. Existing methods couldn't handle this task. They either staggered around like they were drunk, or gamed the problem by dodging the level instead of actually clearing it.

The new method clears levels like a ninja. It combines and adapts the skills it has learned to fit the situation. It holds up well on longer levels, when multiple levels are placed together, and in front of obstacle layouts it has never seen before.

Here's how it works. One character is placed in two classrooms at once. In the first classroom, it imitates human motion. That produces human-like movement, but nothing beyond what it has already seen. In the second classroom, it solves new obstacle courses. Both classrooms feed it information about the body, the obstacles, and the destination together.

The key is a judge. Shown real human motion alongside the surrounding obstacles, the judge has to call it real; shown AI-generated motion, it has to call it fake. That judge is used to train an AI performer. Clumsy movement gets a low score, while human-like movement that fits the obstacles gets rewarded. The performer gets better at fooling the judge, and the judge gets better at catching artificial movement, and the two improve together. A final term stabilizes the judge so that a slight change in movement doesn't flip its verdict entirely.

It's not perfect. Tracking error is lower than with previous methods, but the success rate is a bit lower too. The success rate on long levels still sits around 40%. Unnatural recovery movements also remain a limitation. The paper is freely available, and code may follow later.

blocks.cap: PS5 Pro beta system software update

blocks.x: The feature that ultimately defines the PS5 Pro is a single one: the PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) upscaler. The first version left something to be desired, with cases like the Silent Hill 2 remake where it didn't mesh properly with Unreal Engine 5's lighting rendering. PSSR 2.0, which followed, took the console's gaming experience up a notch.

The problem is games that haven't been updated. Those titles still only support the first version, so improving their image quality depends on the system's “Enhanced PSSR Image Quality” toggle. That toggle will eventually disappear once a successor to the upscaler arrives. Until then, Sony seems intent on getting as much use out of it as possible, so that PS5 Pro users end up using the latest PSSR in every supported game.

According to posts on the ResetERA forum, Sony has started sending out invitations to test a new PlayStation 5 system software update. The accompanying email reads: "The 'Enhanced PSSR Image Quality' feature is now turned on by default. Updating your system software will automatically turn on this setting. When enabled, Enhanced PSSR Image Quality is applied even to games that support an earlier version of PSSR, giving you a sharper, clearer picture."

The rest is quiet: system software performance and stability improvements, plus a small change to the Bluetooth off function in some regions. That said, since this is still a beta, there's room for undocumented features or additional changes before the final release. No official release date has been set yet.

Square Enix, one of Japan's largest game publishers, is teaming up with Google to build AI for QA testing. The goal is to speed things up by automating quality control and review in game development. After AI has already pushed into the roles of artists and programmers across gaming and other industries, QA testers are now on the chopping block.

According to Automaton, Square Enix has been actively using Gemini, Google's flagship AI, to speed up QA testing. At last week's Google Cloud Next Tokyo '26 event, the company confirmed directly that it plans to use more AI in game development.

The AI is said to be able to play through an entire game. It “analyzes the screen and understands what's happening in the game” and uses in-game controls directly. A video reportedly demonstrating this was shown at the event, but the video itself has been hard to actually track down.

blocks.cap: Square Enix is well known for the Final Fantasy series. Now it has AI by its side too. Image credit: Square Enix

blocks.x: Square Enix executives explained that they never envisioned having a conversation with the AI. What they wanted was “an AI that listens to the game's sound, observes minute changes happening on screen, and fully understands the situation.” Automaton noted that the workload on Square Enix developers has grown significantly in recent years, and that this appears to be the backdrop for expanding AI use.
The company says this will let developers focus on creative work and lighten the burden of the most tedious tasks.

In theory, that makes sense, since a large part of QA involves holding down a movement button and repeating the same action endlessly. But it's hard to shake the feeling that this is corporate language covering up the real intent. AI makes things cheap and fast, not necessarily better.

Automaton added that Square Enix even received support from Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry to build an AI-based automated QA development platform. That gives the company institutional backing to push ahead.

In any industry, AI takes human creativity away. Creativity isn't just the basis of art; it underpins countless fields. QA is tedious, grueling work, that much is true, but AI will miss a lot, especially at a fine-grained level, and the result will be a worse experience at launch than before.
On top of that, because AI makes things up so often, cleaning up after it could become an even more tedious and tricky job, likely piling more work onto the very developers it was supposed to help.
Everyone loses out, and these giant companies, backed even by the government, don't so much as blink.

In a recent earnings call for Take-Two Interactive, maker of Grand Theft Auto 6, CEO Strauss Zelnick spoke about the future of AI in game development. While he acknowledged his own company would use AI, he held firm to the view that the technology would not replace anyone.
“Those tools don't replace anybody,” Zelnick said. He explained that the company focuses on making entertainment rather than leading with technology.

“The first of our core pillars is creativity,” Zelnick said. “We have 13,000 colleagues around the world, the vast majority of whom create something every day. I believe technology can enhance their creativity, but it cannot and should not replace it.”

Zelnick does not believe using AI will significantly lower development costs. Instead, he said it could “meaningfully elevate” the quality of games. He has said similar things before. In a 2025 investor presentation, Take-Two said it would not use AI as an excuse to cut staff.

Zelnick also confirmed that day that GTA 6 has not been delayed and will launch on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S on November 19. He forecast that GTA 6 would give the company a very strong fiscal year. He said pre-orders are at a level “unprecedented in the industry,” and may represent demand the industry has never seen.

blocks.cap: Image: Kotaku

blocks.x: Kim Hyung Tae is an artist who has made games for decades. It was never going to go over well with hardcore fans once he embraced generative AI. The Shift Up CEO recently released a music video featuring Evie, the protagonist of the studio's new game Stellar Blade: Blood Rain. Fans kept calling it slop and tearing it down, and his explanation didn't change their minds.

“EVIE, who is the center of this video, is a character our talented artists and modelers spent over a year building from head to toe.” Kim Hyung Tae wrote on X last week, as reported by IGN. “AI isn't creating her from scratch. It's rendering the character based on the data, design, and craftsmanship our team built. I'd really appreciate it if you could view the work with that in mind.”

That explanation only raises more questions about where the finished video actually came from. Was it produced using only existing human-made art and in-game footage? Wasn't the AI tool used trained on a database full of other people's work? How many people actually worked on the music video itself?
One fan answered with a comparison. “Bayonetta pulled this off 16 years ago, without AI, using in-game models, on a far smaller budget than Stellar Blade….”

“Kim Hyung Tae was one of the most influential artists of our generation.” said another fan. “It's absurd that he's defending AI this openly, even at the cost of his reputation. One drawing from you, on skill alone, would spread further than any AI video.” Another post said he'd tainted over a year of work with something as cheap as a “Grok, make my character dance” request.

Some pointed out that Evie in the video doesn't resemble how she looked at her trailer debut earlier this year. “You're diminishing the quality of your own work, your brand, your studio, and the character Evie herself,” one user wrote. Even players with no objection to generative AI itself took issue with the quality of this particular result. “If it had looked good, the reaction would have been positive. But the costume changes between cuts, and so does her appearance. LLMs are improving, but they're not there yet.”

One critic posted this: “Telling a computer to spit out a ridiculously bad AI video and then acting like that is insane self-justification. He's basically saying, 'understand me, I showed you a drawing of my character I made,' lol. The reason the effort looks like zero is that it actually is. Take the hint.”

This is the first time Shift Up has been on the defensive since Stellar Blade launched. The hardcore fandom that spread conspiracy theories about Sony censorship and raged over the game missing out on Game of the Year nominations—with its fierce attachment to the female protagonist in particular—has now turned on the CEO himself.

There's no evidence yet that AI was used in Stellar Blade: Blood Rain itself. But Kim Hyung Tae has been openly pushing the technology as a tool that lets small studios compete with big companies. “We put about 150 people on one game, while China puts in 1,000 to 2,000,” he said earlier this year. “We can't compete on quality or on volume of content.”
“One person can do the work of 100,” he added. Meanwhile, AI can also burn through an entire fandom's goodwill in a matter of seconds.

blocks.cap: Image: Kotaku

blocks.x: Artificial intelligence keeps pushing further into the games industry. Some are still wary of the technology, while several studios are already experimenting with changing how people and virtual worlds connect in the first place. This time, one of the world's leading tech companies has released an ambitious project meant to set the standard for that new wave.

ChinaJoy 2026, one of Asia's biggest gaming events, became a stage where AI-driven projects showed themselves off. One that stood out was World Apart, a PC RPG being made under ByteDance, the owner of TikTok. The company makes no secret of wanting a presence in the games industry too.

The studio's stated goal is bold: to become the game with the most generative AI in the market. It's more of a marketing line than a measurable trait, but it makes clear where the development is headed.

In conventional role-playing games, NPCs repeat lines written in advance. World Apart aims for much more natural conversation. The idea is to have characters read context and respond to player choices in real time, so each encounter plays out differently.

What technology will make this happen hasn't been disclosed yet. But integration with NVIDIA ACE is widely rumored. It's a platform built by the American company to give NPCs advanced conversational ability, having characters listen, process information, and answer with voice generated on the spot.

This isn't the first time. A widely known example is inZOI, made by Krafton. Characters called Smart Zois showed more complex behavior, simulated emotion, and a breadth of interaction rarely seen in this genre.

Interest is high, but World Apart is still full of question marks. The official Steam page confirms only that it's in development and lets people add it to their wishlist, while the combat system, character progression, world scale, and exploration all remain hidden.

Much of the heated anticipation in China comes from exactly that unknown. Most of what's been shown so far is AI-made prerendered footage, and there's been no extended look at how it actually plays. That's why many are asking whether what's visible now is the final product, and whether AI will really turn things upside down the way the studio claims.

World Apart is part of a bigger picture at ByteDance. The company has spent years restructuring its interactive entertainment organization and attaching AI to multiple projects, releasing nearly a dozen titles at ChinaJoy 2026 alone.

What gets said on stage needs to be taken with a grain of salt. Phrases like “the game with the most AI in the world” are familiar marketing language, and there's no evidence yet that the promise will really translate into a different experience. What's clear is that this ranks among the most ambitious generative-AI experiments announced recently. Even meeting part of its goals could mark a line in the evolution of NPCs.

“There's a question I keep turning over these days: how will outside developers use AI tools for the game development and publishing companies that are their clients?” Dean Takahashi opened his August 8 column, The DeanBeat, this way.

blocks.cap: Master Chief in Halo Campaign Evolved. Source: Microsoft

blocks.x: The example he gives is Microsoft. When Microsoft laid off 1,600 people in early July and said it would cut 1,600 (or 1,250) more, Takahashi interviewed outside developers who lost their jobs as a result. The shadow of the layoff decisions fell even on developers who weren't Microsoft employees.

The column asks how the outsourcing and co-development studios that support AAA art and production pipelines will actually deploy AI tools for their publisher clients amid a shrinking ecosystem. The question itself shifts from “Will AI replace developers?” to “Whose pipeline is it when the work sits outside the company?”
The rest of the piece is reserved for GamesBeat's paid membership, GB MAX, so this is as far as the translation goes.

KRAFTON JAPAN held a talk event, “KRAFTON × ReLU Games Development Talk,” in Tokyo on August 5, 2026. Staff from ReLU Games, a creative studio under KRAFTON, ran sessions covering how they use AI in game development, using the development of the PC horror game MIMESIS as a case study.

blocks.cap: MIMESIS

blocks.x: MIMESIS is a four-player co-op horror game pitted against an AI that mimics players. Its core idea is “cooperation with an entity you can't trust”: to survive, players must team up with teammates, yet face the dilemma that the teammate beside them might not be human. The AI-driven NPC, MIMESIS, mimics a player's movement and voice in real time, blending naturally into the group. The game has sold 2 million copies on Steam since its early access launch in October 2025.

AI Creative team leader Lee Gi-mun's session, “A Studio That Produces 3 to 4 Prototypes a Week,” introduced how the studio uses AI. The studio sees AI as bringing a new grammar to games, just as the internet once gave rise to online games and smartphones brought new experiences to mobile games.

blocks.cap: Lee Gi-mun

blocks.x: Right now, though, AI in the world is mostly used just as a tool. Handling a camera requires knowledge of lenses and optics, but that alone doesn't make a good film. To make a good film, you need to learn how to craft a good story. The same goes for AI and game development, Lee Gi-mun said: the question is how to use AI to create new kinds of fun in games — in other words, “AI game design.”

ReLU Games set three principles. First, build a large volume of output bottom-up: any staff member can make, release, and revise a game directly. Second, start from a Seed, not an idea: instead of a design document, make a prototype called a “Seed” that lets people actually play and confirm the fun. Third, focus on solving problems across job boundaries.

To put the three principles into practice, ReLU Games built its own tool, “Nolan.” When a staff member uploads a Seed's source code, AI turns it into something anyone can play and publishes it. Other staff who try it don't just comment on what could be improved — they also use AI agents to attempt to improve the source code itself.

blocks.cap: Nolan's workflow

blocks.x: What matters is that, in Nolan, AI's job is only to build and deploy the source code — people themselves come up with the actual improvements. Leaving build and deployment to AI cuts down on the need for server engineers, letting each staff member release more Seeds in less time. The company has released 114 Seeds internally, all made within five days by a single AI agent specialist.

blocks.cap: Ahn Jae-hong

blocks.x: MIMESIS director Ahn Jae-hong's session, “How a Prototype That Almost Got Buried Was Reborn as a 2-Million-Copy Game,” covered that process. The prototype, “Doppelganger,” was a hardcore escape-action game pitting three players against three doppelgangers. Playtest feedback was mostly negative: people could tell new AI technology was involved, but said the game itself wasn't fun, or that it could have been made without AI technology at all. Development was halted in August 2024. Ahn Jae-hong said that, given limited resources, “without a quick decision, we would have spent a lot more time on the same concept.”
