blocks.cap: A leaked “Project Swan” render. Image: Luna

blocks.x: It's not clear whether the spatial video model is the real reason for that delay. A global component shortage, which has already pushed up prices for RAM, storage, and now Qualcomm SoCs, alongside Valve's standalone headset Steam Frame, could also be holding Pico back.
The company said it will unveil the Pico Space Pro within the fourth quarter. The fourth quarter begins on October 1.

These days, scenes of generative AI operators who treated other people's work as their own colliding head-on with copyright law repeat almost daily. This time it was good news for Genshin Impact developer HoYoverse: a Shanghai court ruled that roughly $112,000 in damages must be paid.

blocks.cap: Genshin Impact characters. Image: MiHoYo

blocks.x: According to a report by Automaton, an unnamed “AI service provider,” also based in Shanghai, must pay 750,000 yuan — the price for reproducing the voices of 63 Genshin Impact characters without authorization.

The court found that the AI voice packs the company sold had “nearly identical characteristics” to the gacha game's characters. For promotion, it used slightly altered versions of the character images.

The Shanghai Pudong New Area People's Court therefore ruled that the infringement extended beyond in-game content to the character designs themselves, concluding it amounted to unfair competition. The voice packs' intended use had little to do with ordinary Genshin Impact play; the product presented slightly altered versions of the characters as chatty virtual avatars.

In any case, HoYoverse won this round, though the $112,000 it recovered is far less than it was hoping for. The company, which also makes Honkai: Star Rail, originally sought 5 million yuan, about $745,000, along with an immediate injunction.
Instead of awarding the full amount, the court ordered the infringing conduct to stop immediately. Now that the AI company recently withdrew its appeal, the $112,000 payment is final.
Mages has long held the position of Japan's most beloved visual novel developer. Stories like Steins;Gate succeeded internationally even after moving beyond games into anime.

It's not as if the company never touched other genres; it released a rhythm game last year. Still, its name has always meant meticulously crafted visual novels, or small spin-offs of its latest anime. That's exactly why it's so strange that the new game Juggernaut is an AI clone of Quake.

blocks.cap: Juggernaut, the AI shooter Mages unveiled. Image: Mages

blocks.x: The reveal came fairly abruptly on the company's social media account. Juggernaut bills itself as a return to “the '90s,” saying it “looks retro and plays retro, because it is retro.”

Even a brief look at the screen leaves a strange impression of Quake and Doom mixed with zombies. The goal is simply to kill 5,000 enemies. The particular smoothness of AI-generated art makes everything look slightly off.

blocks.cap: The result of a leap into a genre it had never touched. Image: Mages

blocks.x: The answer lies in the AI disclosure on the Steam page. The secret to leaping so smoothly into a genre it had never touched was heavy use of AI technology. The company stated that it used generative AI models to create 100 percent of the game's source code and effects, 60 percent of the graphics, and 50 percent of the sound.
Reaction from English-speaking fans has been close to unanimously negative, with voices criticizing the game's look alongside others surprised that AI was involved in development to this extent.

Mages isn't the only Japanese studio eyeing generative AI. A survey last year found that 51 percent of Japanese game studios were experimenting with the technology, and some, like Level-5, have openly shown how they used generated assets.

Still, going so far as to make an entire game with AI and release it is rare. It's hard to find a reason to pick Juggernaut over the games it so obviously copies. For now, it can only be added to a wishlist, and there's no release date yet.
